claim: Developer-run argument-mapping courses (Reason!/Melbourne, Monash) show about 0.7 to 0.9 SD pre/post gains on the CCTST in one semester (d 0.73 to 0.89 across the 2000-2002 Reason! cohorts, pooled N=232 in van Gelder 2004).
agent_test: none (descriptive history)

claim: The causal claim that mapping itself, not extra practice time, maturation or retesting, causes the gain is NOT established: no randomised trial; the founders estimate about 0.3 SD would occur anyway; the no-map control in Dwyer 2012 rose d=.55; Peer Instruction gave d=.40 vs mapping d=.45.
agent_test: Equal-token A/B on one task class: (i) plain CoT, (ii) CoT plus an explicit map step, (iii) CoT plus an equal-length free-form outline. Only (ii) > (iii) supports a map-specific effect.

claim: Independent replications give smaller effects than the developers: Butchart (Monash, 2009) 0.45 SD with automated feedback and 0.19 for the standard course; Dwyer (thesis) found no overall CT gain from mapping over hierarchical outlining or controls; Harrell found a gain only for low-pretest students; one MANCOVA dissertation (snippet only) found no effect. Harrell 2011 re-read: overall gain difference was 0.22 vs 0.18 in both studies and not significant (t(53)=1.35; t(126)=1.22).
agent_test: Treat the 0.8 SD figure as an upper bound; expect a small or zero average effect on a strong model and test per task class.

claim: Dose: hours of software practice correlate with gain about r=0.31, and high users gained 5.17 vs 2.38 CCTST points in 2002 (median split at 8.84 h). This is correlational (motivated students practise more).
agent_test: Not testable on an LLM as stated; the analogue is number of map revisions and map size at equal tokens.

claim: Lower starting skill is associated with bigger gains, but the evidence is mixed: Reason! pretest-gain r=-0.54 (N=281); Harrell 2011 low-pretest gain 0.40 vs 0.28 (Study 1, n=6 vs 32, p=.14, n.s.) and 0.39 vs 0.24 (Study 2, n=24 vs 22, p=.007); the intermediate-group benefit appeared in Study 1 only. Regression to the mean is a rival explanation. The earlier 'd=1.1' figure for Harrell low students was not found in the paper text.
agent_test: Gate S2 mapping on a difficulty or inconsistency signal (G12 spirit) and compare with mapping every item.

claim: Feedback matters: automated feedback on maps gave d=0.45 vs 0.22 without feedback (different semesters, not randomised; CI +/-0.29 on the feedback arm). Indirect LLM support: intrinsic self-critique without an outside signal lowers accuracy (GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8) while oracle feedback raises it (GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3).
agent_test: Check that a map revision cites the located failing output (G2) vs a self-critique of the map at equal tokens.

claim: Mapping versus plain outlining: no consistent advantage. Dwyer Exp 4 map vs summarising d=1.30 but outline vs summarising d=.84; AM vs hierarchical outline showed no difference on recall or most CT subscales.
agent_test: Compare a typed graph (claims, support, objection) with a flat bulleted decomposition at equal tokens.

claim: Pooled meta-analytic support is weak: Alvarez-Ortiz (2007) reports 0.68 SD (some mapping) and 0.78 (LAMP) vs 0.30 (some CT), but only via a thesis and built on uncontrolled studies. A 2026 review calls the pooled effect large without a number we could read; the 2025 scoping review judges pooling impractical. Gap search: the 2025 review (124 studies) reports no pooled effect in its abstract and the 2026 chapter is by a Reason!/Rationale developer; neither could be read for numbers.
agent_test: None (literature fact); do not import 0.78 SD as a prior.

claim: Mapping does not change thinking dispositions: need for cognition and motivation unchanged; reflective-judgement follow-up showed no group effect; the AOMT disposition exercises gave d=0.14.
agent_test: Not applicable to an LLM; skill gains cannot be expected to come with a disposition shift.

claim: Only near transfer is shown: outcomes are the CCTST, map scores themselves (d=0.91, no control) or recall; follow-up retention rests on a self-selected n=20; reviews say outcomes are mostly perception or essay scores.
agent_test: Measure transfer for any map step: tune its prompt on one task class, test on another.

claim: Map benefit has a size ceiling: recall advantage shrank at 50 vs 30 propositions (Dwyer), and users of LLM rationale graphs reported node text overload and navigation cost.
agent_test: Cap map size (nodes) and test accuracy as nodes grow at equal tokens; compare pruned vs full map.

claim: Using a map as a scaffold for an LLM (pro and con argument graphs, DF-QuAD aggregation) gives accuracy at best equal to chain of thought zero-shot: GPT-4o MedClaim 0.85 direct, 0.85 CoT, 0.83 ArgLLM depth 1 (verified in the paper table); 0.5-base ArgLLM usually below CoT; depth 2 no better; a separate study found direct prompting beat more complex UQ methods.
agent_test: Replicate on our task class: CoT vs argument-graph prompting at equal tokens; expect parity, so any map step must be justified by other benefits (contestability, error location).

claim: Argument-graph approaches can beat baselines when extra components are added: MArgE up to about 20% over comparison methods with a stronger scorer; a fact-checking framework +5.39 and +11.10 macro-F1 over best baseline, partly from adversarial retrieval. The map alone is not isolated.
agent_test: Ablate the retrieval or scorer from the map to see what carries the gain.

claim: Graph structure of an LLM reasoning trace carries a correctness signal: argument-graph uncertainty had the highest prediction rejection rate in 8 of 9 models on GPQA Diamond (Nemotron-30B 0.65 vs 0.24 consistency; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B 0.34 vs 0.46, the exception; blend 0.68 for Nemotron; verified in the paper table); trace-graph exploration density correlated r=0.68 with accuracy.
agent_test: Use a code-computed graph feature as one selection hint in S7, tested against sample consistency; per G4 it is a hint, not proof.

claim: Structured step-graph verification helps some models but not all: Graph of Verification lifted ProcessBench F1 for Qwen2.5-32B (OlympiadBench 35.9 to 65.2, MATH 49.4 to 72.7) but not Llama3.3-70B on GSM8K (78.6 to 78.6); synthetic arithmetic with injected errors showed larger gains.
agent_test: At S8, compare a step-DAG verifier with a holistic verifier on our model at equal tokens.

claim: Showing humans a graph of an LLM rationale changes trust calibration only on hard verbal tasks (hard BBH: over-trust beta -0.199, error correction +0.182, verified) and hurts on visual I-RAVEN (appropriate trust -0.165); subjective ratings split from objective ones. Single online study, N=204 valid of 223.
agent_test: Only relevant if a human reads our maps; our agent does not use human trust.

claim: LLM argument mining works at component level but not end-to-end: conclusion detection accuracy 92.50%, relation accuracy 80.57% on textbook arguments; on AbstRCT the full pipeline span F1 59.65 vs 70.93 for a supervised model; exact-match scoring penalises valid alternative segmentations. Surveys agree few studies test quality in downstream pipelines.
agent_test: Build the map with code-checked structure (schema validation) and measure parse-failure rate, since unconstrained LLM mapping varies across seeds.

claim: No study was found that tests an LLM on van Gelder-style argument-mapping training or that measures whether LLM-built maps improve the same LLM's reasoning at equal tokens; LLM-made maps for students appear only as demos or tiny cases (N=17). The search was thin (APIs rate-limited), so this is absence of evidence found, not proof. Gap search closest tests: Argument Generation (pro/con) and Critical-Questions-of-Thought, neither is a full map or equal-token.
agent_test: This is the direct experiment to run: map-first vs CoT at equal tokens on a held-out task class.

claim: Teaching an LLM to coach argument quality (not map drawing) improved tutor metrics: up to 53% above base on average with normal students; adversarial student divergence 84.0 vs 38.0; plain LLM tutors conceded to the student stance in 85% of pilot cases. Small human check N=20.
agent_test: Related to sycophancy; not a test of mapping.

claim: Pro/con argument generation before answering beats zero-shot CoT on average only for small and medium models (mean gain 3.18% small, 2.72% medium, 0.95% large, nine tasks, ten models); chain of thought wins on several tasks. Equal tokens were not controlled in the text read.
agent_test: Run the K02 three-arm test and report gain by model size; expect a gate for weaker passes.

claim: Asking critical questions drawn from Toulmin's model before answering raised GPT-4o-judge scores in 18 of 20 model-domain cells (40 questions per model) but costs many extra calls, has no significance tests, and CoT won for Nemotron on reasoning (7.7 vs 7.3).
agent_test: Compare a critical-question loop with an equal-call free-form self-critique on a task with code-checkable answers.

claim: Intrinsic self-critique without an external failure signal does not improve reasoning and often hurts (GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8 after two rounds; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0), while oracle labels give large gains (GPT-3.5 GSM8K 84.3, GPT-4 HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0). So a revision step needs a located failure from code or a checker.
agent_test: Map revision driven by a failing test vs a self-critique of the map, equal tokens.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-20 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Sample agreement is a cheap code-computed confidence signal (self-consistency, GSM8K +17.9 over CoT); any graph-feature selection hint from a single trace must beat it, and one study found it did not for R1-Distill-Llama-70B.
agent_test: Select among N candidates by sample consistency vs by graph-structure features; report both.

claim: A reusable code-aggregated argument graph per decision option (ArgEval) gave similar label-match to the base LLM (0.8818 vs 0.8630 Qwen3-30B; 0.8485 best vs 0.8775 gpt-oss-20b) with 2.4x fewer completion tokens at depth 2, but variants ranged 0.4432 to 0.8485 on gpt-oss-20b. Benefit is cost and contestability, not accuracy.
agent_test: Build the map once per task class with code-validated format; compare cost and accuracy against per-item reasoning.

claim: A justification written after the verdict can use a different argument scheme from the reasoning that produced it: about 20% per model across nine frontier models and 200 dilemmas. A map built after the answer is therefore not evidence of how the answer was reached.
agent_test: Build the map before answering and check by code that the final choice follows from the map.

claim: No randomised, actively controlled trial of argument mapping on a standardised critical-thinking test was found in this gap pass; the only controlled designs seen are quasi-experimental (Harrell, intact classes) or unreachable (Dwyer 81-student chapter, snippet only). Gaps 1 and 2 remain open.
agent_test: none (absence of evidence)
